title: Andromache. Helenus vates
titleEn: Andromache and the Prophecy of Helenus — Aeneid III.306–409
part: Andromache and the Prophecy of Helenus (III.306–409)
about: Aeneas, still telling Dido of his wanderings, comes to Buthrotum in Epirus, where Helenus, a son of Priam, now reigns over a small copy of Troy. By the dry bed of a stream called Xanthus, at a cenotaph of Hector, he finds Hector's widow Andromache, who faints at the sight of him and then asks, in broken questions, whether he is alive and what fortune has brought him there. She tells her own story: Polyxena at least was spared slavery; she herself was carried off by Achilles' son Pyrrhus, who passed her on to Helenus when he went after Hermione; Orestes killed Pyrrhus at the altar, and Helenus inherited part of his kingdom. She breaks off asking after Ascanius. Helenus arrives, weeping, and the Trojans are feasted in his halls. When the wind calls them on, Aeneas asks the seer, who serves Apollo, how to escape the perils Celaeno foretold. Helenus performs the rites, leads him to the god's temple, and speaks. He will not tell everything, for the Fates and Juno forbid it, but he gives the great outline: Italy is far off, there are seas to cross, Sicily to pass, the underworld to visit and Circe's island to clear before a city can be founded; the sign will be a white sow with thirty young beside a river; the gnawing of the tables will not hurt; and the nearest coast of Italy is full of Greek settlements to avoid. He ends with the rule that Aeneas must veil his head when he sacrifices, a Roman custom that his descendants should keep. Helenus's speech goes on into the next part.

sentences.i: When she caught sight of me approaching, and, out of her wits, saw Trojan arms all around me, she was appalled by portents so great and stiffened in the very midst of her gaze; the warmth went out of her bones;
sentences.n: Aeneas goes on telling Dido the story. The subject 'she' (Andromache) is not named: the last part showed her at a cenotaph of Hector by a copy of the river Xanthus, and the Trojan arms she sees are Aeneas's own and his men's. 'Ut… conspexit… vidit' — 'when she caught sight of'; 'ut' with the perfect indicative means 'when'. 'me venientem' — 'me coming', a present participle agreeing with 'me'. 'Troïa circum arma' — 'Troïa' is an adjective with 'arma', set ahead of the preposition 'circum' that governs 'arma' ('round about the Trojan arms'); the dots over the i (diaeresis) show that 'Troïa' is three syllables, Tro-ï-a. 'amens' is nominative, with 'she': out of her mind. 'magnis exterrita monstris' — 'exterrita' is a perfect passive participle, 'terrified', and 'monstris' (ablative of cause) are marvels, sights against nature. 'deriguit' is the perfect of 'derigesco', 'stiffen with fear'. 'visu in medio' — 'in the middle of the seeing'. The last clause has no connecting word (asyndeton), which gives the effect of sudden shock.

sentences.t: labitur, et longo vix tandem tempore fatur:
sentences.l: she slips, and after a long time, hardly at last, speaks:
sentences.i: She sinks, and only after a long while, and with difficulty, does she speak:
sentences.n: 'labitur' is the present of the deponent 'labor', 'slip, glide down'; she is collapsing, fainting. The present tense is the 'historic present', used for vivid narration, and runs through the whole scene. 'longo vix tandem tempore' — 'after a long time, scarcely at last'; three words that all say 'finally, with trouble'. 'fatur' is the deponent 'for, fari', 'to speak', a solemn word that goes with speech of weight (you'll see it again as 'fare' in line 362). The colon introduces her words.

sentences.t:
“Verane te facies, verus mihi nuntius adfers,
nate dea?
sentences.l:
“Is it as a true form, as a true messenger to me, that you bring yourself,
son of a goddess?
sentences.i: “Is it as a true form, a true messenger, that you come to me, son of a goddess?
sentences.n: Andromache's questions run to the end of line 312, where her first speech ends. 'Verane' — 'vera' with the question-marker '-ne' attached to it; the first word of a question gets the '-ne' (the same as 'Vivisne', 'mene' in the pilot). 'te… adfers' — 'adfero' with a reflexive object, 'bring yourself, present yourself'; 'facies' and 'nuntius' are what you present yourself as, 'a true form, a true messenger'; she is afraid he is a ghost. 'nate dea' — 'nate' is the vocative of 'natus', 'son', and 'dea' is the ablative of origin, with no preposition: 'son (born) of a goddess', that is, of Venus. A poetic address that returns in 374. 'verus… verus' — the repetition of 'vera' and 'verus' shows how badly she wants it to be true.

sentences.t:
Vivisne, aut, si lux alma recessit,
Hector ubi est?
sentences.l:
Do you live? or, if the kindly light has departed,
where is Hector?”
sentences.i: Are you alive? Or, if the kindly light of life has left you, where is Hector?”
sentences.n: 'Vivisne' — 'vivis' with '-ne', 'do you live?'. 'aut, si lux alma recessit' — 'or, if the kindly light has gone', that is, if you are dead; the light is the light of the living world, and 'alma' ('nourishing, kindly') is a standing epithet. 'recessit' is perfect indicative in the condition: she regards it as a real possibility. 'Hector ubi est' — 'ubi' stands after its subject, the order in which the thought comes to her; Hector's name is the one that matters. The closing speech mark ” stands in Greenough's text before the next word (like 'pios! ”Tum' earlier), so the next unit's Latin begins with it.

sentences.t:
”Dixit, lacrimasque effudit et omnem
implevit clamore locum.
sentences.l:
She spoke, and poured out tears and all
the place she filled with her outcry.
sentences.i: She spoke, and burst into tears, and filled the whole place with her cries.
sentences.n: Speech ends and the narrator, Aeneas, resumes. 'Dixit' is the usual closing word for a speech (you'll see it constantly). 'Dixit… effudit… implevit' — three perfects, joined by '-que' and 'et'; 'omnem… locum' frames the line break (hyperbaton): 'omnem' ends line 312 and 'locum' ends 313, as all the place is filled. 'clamore' is an ablative of means. Andromache's grief is a Homeric theme: in the Iliad she laments Hector before he dies (6) and after (22, 24).

sentences.t:
Vix pauca furenti
subicio, et raris turbatus vocibus hisco:
sentences.l:
Scarcely a few things to her raving
I put in reply, and, shaken, in scanty words I falter:
sentences.i: To her frenzy I can answer only a few words, and, shaken, I falter them out in broken speech:
sentences.n: 'Vix pauca furenti subicio' — 'I hardly throw in a few things to (her) raving'; 'furenti' is a present participle in the dative, 'to her being frantic', and 'subicio' means 'put under, put in after'. 'raris turbatus vocibus' — 'turbatus' is a perfect passive participle (nominative, with 'I'): 'shaken'; 'raris vocibus' (ablative) — 'with scanty, sparse words'. 'hisco' is 'to open the mouth, gape', here 'to say with difficulty'. A colon follows because Aeneas's reply comes next.

sentences.t: Vivo equidem, vitamque extrema per omnia duco;
sentences.l: “I live indeed, and life through every extremity I lead;
sentences.i: “I live, truly — I am drawing out my life through every extremity;
sentences.n: The print has no opening speech mark before Aeneas's reply, a misprint (an omission) for “, corrected in the translation; the Latin is left as printed, and the closing mark at 319 shows that the reply runs 315–319. 'Vivo equidem' — 'equidem' is a strong 'indeed, for my part'. 'vitam… duco' — 'I lead (draw out) my life', a regular phrase. 'extrema per omnia' — 'extrema' is an adjective with 'omnia', 'all the extremes', and 'per' is set between them: 'through every extremity'. Aeneas answers her first question (are you alive?), and the next words answer her fear that he is a vision.

sentences.t: ne dubita, nam vera vides.
sentences.l: do not doubt, for true things you see.
sentences.i: have no doubt — what you see is real.
sentences.n: A half-line: Virgil left some lines unfinished (this is one of the 'hemistichs', about 58 in the poem), and Greenough prints it short. 'ne dubita' — 'ne' with the imperative is a poetic way to say a negative command, instead of 'noli dubitare'; 'nam vera vides' — 'for you see true things', neuter plural used as a noun. It also seems a reply to 'Verane… facies' of line 310.

sentences.t:
Heu, quis te casus deiectam coniuge tanto
excipit, aut quae digna satis fortuna revisit
Hectoris Andromachen?
sentences.l:
Alas, what chance receives you, cast down from so great a husband,
or what fortune worthy enough revisits
Hector's Andromache?
sentences.i: Alas, what chance has caught you, brought down from so great a husband? Or what fortune, worthy enough, comes once more to Hector's Andromache?
sentences.n: 'Heu' is an exclamation of grief. 'quis… casus' — 'quis' is the interrogative adjective, 'what chance'. 'te… deiectam coniuge tanto' — 'deiectam' is a perfect passive participle (accusative, with 'te'), 'thrown down'; 'coniuge tanto' is an ablative of separation without a preposition, 'from so great a husband'. 'excipit' means 'receives, takes in, catches', as in catching someone who has fallen. 'quae digna satis fortuna' — 'what fortune worthy enough (of you)'. 'revisit' — 'revisits', the sense of coming again to someone. 'Hectoris Andromachen' — 'Andromachen' is a Greek accusative singular in -en; the Latin Library prints 'Andromache', which would not suit the object of 'revisit'.

sentences.t: Pyrrhin’ conubia servas?”
sentences.l: Of Pyrrhus — do you keep the wedlock?”
sentences.i: Are you still bound in marriage to Pyrrhus?”
sentences.n: 'Pyrrhin’' is 'Pyrrhi' ('of Pyrrhus', genitive) with '-ne' attached, the question marker, the 'e' of '-ne' lost before the consonant of 'conubia' (the apostrophe marks the loss); 'conubia' is plural for singular, 'wedlock, marriage', and 'servas' means 'keep, maintain'. Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, who killed Priam (2.526–558) and took Andromache as a prize. The closing mark ” ends the speech that began without a mark at 315 (see the note there); Andromache replies at once.

sentences.t: Deiecit vultum et demissa voce locuta est:
sentences.l: She cast down her face and with lowered voice spoke:
sentences.i: She lowered her face and answered in a low voice:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a new speaker begins (the narrator, Aeneas, introduces her). 'Deiecit vultum' — 'vultum' is 'face, look', and 'deiecit' — 'threw down', the same verb as 'deiectam' above; she casts her eyes down in shame and grief. 'demissa voce' — 'demissa' is a perfect passive participle, 'let down, lowered', in the ablative with 'voce' ('with lowered voice'). 'locuta est' is a deponent perfect. The next 23 lines are one long speech by Andromache (321–343); her anguish is shown in the way it breaks and reverses.

sentences.t:
“O felix una ante alias Priameïa virgo,
hostilem ad tumulum Troiae sub moenibus altis
iussa mori, quae sortitus non pertulit ullos,
nec victoris eri tetigit captiva cubile!
sentences.l:
“O fortunate one beyond all the others, Priam's maiden,
to a hostile tomb beneath Troy's lofty walls
bidden to die, who endured no casting of lots,
and did not touch, a captive, a victor-master's bed!
sentences.i: “O blessed, alone beyond all others, maiden of Priam's house, who were ordered to die at an enemy's tomb beneath the high walls of Troy, who never endured the drawing of lots, nor, a captive, touched the bed of a victorious master!
sentences.n: 'felix' is a vocative (the same as the nominative): 'O fortunate (girl)'. 'una ante alias' — 'one before others', that is, above all others. 'Priameïa virgo' — Priam's daughter Polyxena, sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles after Troy fell (a tradition from the Greek tragedians); 'Priameïa' is five syllables, Pri-a-me-ï-a (the diaeresis shows it). 'hostilem ad tumulum' — 'ad' follows its adjective (hyperbaton): 'to the enemy's tomb'. 'iussa mori' — 'iussa' perfect passive participle, 'having been ordered', with the infinitive 'mori', 'to die'. 'quae sortitus non pertulit ullos' — 'who did not go through any drawings of lots': after the sack, the captive women were assigned to the Greek leaders by lot; Polyxena was spared that. 'nec victoris eri tetigit captiva cubile' — 'eri' is the genitive of 'erus', 'master' (Latin Library has 'heri', same word with its h); 'captiva' is nominative, 'as a captive'. The idea that dying is a mercy next to slavery is for Virgil an old one (Euripides' Hecuba, Trojan Women) and Andromache's bitterness fills the speech.

sentences.t:
nos, patria incensa, diversa per aequora vectae,
stirpis Achilleae fastus iuvenemque superbum,
servitio enixae, tulimus:
sentences.l:
we, our country burned, across scattered seas carried,
the Achillean line's arrogance and the haughty youth,
in slavery having given birth, endured:
sentences.i: As for us, after our country was burned we were carried over scattered seas, and in slavery we gave birth, and bore the pride of Achilles' line and the arrogance of that young man:
sentences.n: 'nos' stands at the front for emphasis, set against Polyxena. 'patria incensa' is an ablative absolute, 'the fatherland (having been) burned'. 'diversa per aequora vectae' — 'vectae' is a perfect passive participle, feminine plural (the Trojan women), 'carried'; 'per' stands between its adjective and noun, 'across' the 'diversa', 'scattered, far-flung' seas. 'stirpis Achilleae fastus iuvenemque superbum… tulimus' — 'fastus' (accusative plural, 'arrogance') and 'iuvenem' are both objects of 'tulimus' ('we endured'); 'stirpis Achilleae' = 'of Achilles' line' (genitive); the haughty youth is Neoptolemus, Achilles's son. 'servitio enixae' — 'enixae' from 'enitor', 'give birth', is a perfect participle with 'nos'; 'servitio' is ablative, 'in slavery'. In the tradition she bore Pyrrhus a son, Molossus; here the birth is mentioned only in passing, as a participle. The colon opens an account of what the youth did next.

sentences.t:
qui deinde, secutus
Ledaeam Hermionen Lacedaemoniosque hymenaeos,
me famulo famulamque Heleno transmisit habendam.
sentences.l:
who then, having pursued
Leda's Hermione and the Lacedaemonian wedding,
me, a slave woman, to Helenus, a slave, passed on to be held.
sentences.i: Then he went after Hermione, Leda's granddaughter, and a Spartan marriage, and handed me over, a slave-woman, to Helenus, himself a slave, to have as his own.
sentences.n: 'qui' is a connecting relative, 'he, who'. 'secutus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'sequor', 'having followed', here 'having gone after'. 'Ledaeam Hermionen' — Hermione was daughter of Helen, who was daughter of Leda; the adjective 'Ledaeam' is used for the family. 'Hermionen' is a Greek accusative. 'Lacedaemoniosque hymenaeos' — 'a Spartan wedding'. 'me famulo famulamque Heleno' — an interlaced arrangement: 'me… famulam' (accusative, 'me, a slave woman') alternates with 'famulo… Heleno' (dative, 'to Helenus, a slave'), setting the two slaves side by side. 'transmisit habendam' — 'habendam' is a gerundive agreeing with 'me' ('famulam'), 'to be held, to be had', a legal word for property.

sentences.t:
Ast illum, ereptae magno inflammatus amore
coniugis et scelerum Furiis agitatus, Orestes
excipit incautum patriasque obtruncat ad aras.
sentences.l:
But him, of the snatched-away wife with great love inflamed
and by the Furies of his crimes driven, Orestes
waylays unwary and cuts down at the ancestral altars.
sentences.i: But Orestes, fired with great love for the wife who had been taken from him and driven by the Furies of his crimes, takes Pyrrhus unawares and cuts him down at the altars of his fathers.
sentences.n: 'Ast' is an old form of 'at', 'but'. 'illum… incautum' — 'him, unwary'. 'ereptae… coniugis' — 'ereptae' is a perfect passive participle, 'snatched away'; Hermione had been promised to Orestes before Pyrrhus married her. 'inflammatus' — 'inflamed'; the Latin Library prints 'flammatus', same sense. 'scelerum Furiis agitatus' — 'driven by the Furies of crimes', that is, those that avenge his crime, the murder of his mother Clytemnestra. 'excipit… obtruncat' — 'excipit' here is 'ambushes, catches'; 'obtruncat', 'cuts down', both in the historic present. 'patrias ad aras' — 'patrias' is 'of his fathers, ancestral'; Virgil does not name the place, and the better-known tradition puts the killing at Delphi, at Apollo's altar; 'ad' stands between adjective and noun, as often. The Orestes story, with the Furies, is again the Greek tragedians' story.

sentences.t:
Morte Neoptolemi regnorum reddita cessit
pars Heleno, qui Chaonios cognomine campos
Chaoniamque omnem Troiano a Chaone dixit,
Pergamaque Iliacamque iugis hanc addidit arcem.
sentences.l:
With the death of Neoptolemus, of the kingdoms handed back, there passed
a part to Helenus, who the Chaonian plains by name
and all Chaonia from Trojan Chaon called,
and Pergamum and, on the ridges, this Ilian citadel added.
sentences.i: At the death of Neoptolemus a share of his realm passed to Helenus, who named the plains Chaonian and the whole country Chaonia after Chaon of Troy, and added a Pergamum, this Trojan citadel, on the ridges.
sentences.n: 'Morte Neoptolemi' — 'Neoptolemus' is Pyrrhus's other name. 'regnorum reddita cessit pars Heleno' — 'reddita' is a perfect passive participle, 'handed over, given up', agreeing with 'pars' ('a part… handed over'), and 'cessit' ('passed') takes a dative 'Heleno'; the 'regnorum' is the genitive of the whole, 'of the kingdoms'. 'qui Chaonios cognomine campos… dixit' — 'dixit' here means 'named' and 'cognomine' (ablative) 'by the name', 'Chaonios' the adjective: Helenus named the plains. 'Troiano a Chaone' — in the tradition Chaon was Helenus's brother, killed by accident while hunting. 'Pergamaque Iliacamque… arcem' — 'Pergama' (neuter plural) is the citadel of Troy, and 'Iliacam arcem', 'the Ilian citadel', stands in apposition to it; 'hanc' — 'this' citadel, the one before their eyes. 'iugis' — 'on the ridges' (ablative of place).

sentences.t: Sed tibi qui cursum venti, quae fata dedere?
sentences.l: But to you what winds a course, what fates have given?
sentences.i: But what winds, what fates, have set you on this course?
sentences.n: She turns from her own story to his. 'qui' is the masculine plural of the interrogative adjective ('quis, qui'), 'what winds', and 'quae' agrees with 'fata'. 'cursum dedere' — 'dedere' is 'dederunt' (the ending -ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly). 'tibi' goes with 'dedere', 'gave you'. The pair 'venti… fata' reflects a question that will be asked often in the poem: is the journey chance or fate?

sentences.t: Aut quisnam ignarum nostris deus adpulit oris?
sentences.l: Or what god, pray, you unknowing to our shores has driven?
sentences.i: Or what god, pray, brought you, unknowing, to our shores?
sentences.n: 'quisnam' is 'quis' with '-nam', 'who, pray?'. 'ignarum' (accusative, 'te' understood) — 'unknowing', that is, you did not know where you were. 'adpulit' — 'drove to' (Greenough's 'adpulit', the Latin Library's 'appulit'); the verb is 'adpello', which is used of ships driven to a coast. 'nostris… oris' — a dative of goal after a compound verb, a poetic use, 'to our shores'. Andromache asks if this is an accident or a god's doing.

sentences.t: Quid puer Ascanius?
sentences.l: What of the boy Ascanius?
sentences.i: And what of the boy Ascanius?
sentences.n: 'Quid puer Ascanius?' has no verb: 'what (is the news) of…?', 'what about…?', a colloquial sort of question that gives the speech its breathless feeling. 'Ascanius', Aeneas's son, who was a boy when Troy fell, was last seen in Book II, where his flaming hair was an omen. She asks after him.

sentences.t:
superatne et vescitur aura,
quem tibi iam Troia—
sentences.l:
does he survive and feed on the breeze,
whom to you already Troy —
sentences.i: Does he live and breathe the air, the boy whom Troy already —
sentences.n: 'superatne' — 'superat' with '-ne': 'does he survive?'. 'vescitur aura' — 'vescor' takes an ablative, 'feeds on the air', a way to say 'breathes, lives'. 'quem tibi iam Troia—' is a half-line (hemistich) and breaks off in the middle of the sentence, with no verb (aposiopesis, 'becoming silent'); Greenough's dash marks it. The Latin does not say how it would have gone on, and it is not completed here; ancient commentators mention that some copies carry a supplied ending, which is not Virgil's. Grief simply stops her.

sentences.t: Ecqua tamen puero est amissae cura parentis?
sentences.l: Is there yet in the boy any care of his lost parent?
sentences.i: Still, does the boy feel any concern for the mother he lost?
sentences.n: 'Ecqua' is 'any?', the interrogative adjective agreeing with 'cura'. 'puero est… cura' — a dative of possession ('to the boy there is a care', the pattern 'sunt mihi', you'll see this constantly). 'amissae parentis' — 'amissae' is a perfect passive participle, 'lost', genitive; 'parentis' is a 'parent', here the mother (Creusa, lost in the flight from Troy, 2.738). 'cura parentis' — an objective genitive: care for her. Andromache, who has lost her own child (Astyanax, thrown from the walls) and Hector, asks about the boy who is also motherless.

sentences.t:
Ecquid in antiquam virtutem animosque virilis
et pater Aeneas et avunculus excitat Hector?”
sentences.l:
Does to ancient valour and manly spirits
both father Aeneas and uncle Hector rouse him?”
sentences.i: And do his father Aeneas, and his uncle Hector, stir him at all to the valour of old and to a manly heart?”
sentences.n: 'Ecquid' is the neuter accusative of 'ecquis', used as an adverb, 'at all?'. 'in antiquam virtutem animosque virilis' — 'in' with the accusative, 'to'; 'antiquam virtutem' is 'ancient valour', the courage of his line; 'virilis' is the accusative plural (the -is ending for -es: you'll see this constantly), 'manly spirits'. 'et pater Aeneas et avunculus… Hector' — 'et… et', 'both… and'; 'avunculus' is a mother's brother: Creusa was Priam's daughter, so Hector was her brother (the child's maternal uncle). The verb 'excitat' is singular, agreeing with the nearer subject. Hector as exemplar for the boy is Andromache's last thought, and a bitter one: the model has died. Her speech ends here, with the closing mark ”.

sentences.t:
Talia fundebat lacrimans longosque ciebat
incassum fletus, cum sese a moenibus heros
Priamides multis Helenus comitantibus adfert,
adgnoscitque suos, laetusque ad limina ducit,
et multum lacrimas verba inter singula fundit.
sentences.l:
Such things she was pouring out, weeping, and long she was rousing
in vain her sobs, when from the walls the hero,
Priam's son Helenus, with many accompanying, brings himself,
and recognises his own, and glad leads them to the thresholds,
and much weeping between single words pours out.
sentences.i: So she spoke through her tears, and long she went on raising her lament in vain, when the hero Helenus, son of Priam, came from the walls with a great company, knew his own people, and led them gladly to his threshold, shedding many a tear between each word.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Talia fundebat lacrimans' — 'fundebat' is imperfect: 'she was pouring out'; the imperfect fits a scene that is still going on when something else happens. 'longos… fletus ciebat incassum' — 'ciebat' is 'was stirring, calling forth' her sobs, 'in vain' ('incassum', adverb). 'cum… adfert' — a 'cum' with the indicative that introduces the main event ('when, suddenly…'); the historic present continues. 'sese… adfert' — 'brings himself', that is, 'arrives'. 'Priamides' is a patronymic, 'son of Priam'. 'multis comitantibus' is an ablative absolute, 'many accompanying'. 'adgnoscitque suos' — 'suos', 'his own people', the Trojans. 'multum' is an adverb, 'much', and 'verba inter singula' is anastrophe again: 'between single words'. Helenus, a son of Priam and a seer, rules this miniature Troy.

sentences.t:
Procedo, et parvam Troiam simulataque magnis
Pergama, et arentem Xanthi cognomine rivum
adgnosco, Scaeaeque amplector limina portae.
sentences.l:
I advance, and little Troy and, imitated to the great ones,
Pergama, and the dry stream, by name of Xanthus,
I recognise, and the Scaean gate's threshold I embrace.
sentences.i: I go forward, and I recognise a little Troy, a Pergamum made in the likeness of the great, and a dry brook that bears the name of Xanthus, and I embrace the threshold of a Scaean gate.
sentences.n: 'Procedo' — 'I go forward'. 'parvam Troiam simulataque magnis Pergama' — 'simulata' is a perfect passive participle, 'made like, imitated', with the dative 'magnis': the 'Pergama' (neuter plural; the citadel of Troy) are 'imitated for the great ones'. 'arentem Xanthi cognomine rivum' — 'arentem' is a present participle, 'drying, dry'; 'cognomine' (ablative) 'by the name' with 'Xanthi' (genitive, the Trojan river); the stream is called Xanthus in memory of the Trojan one. 'adgnosco' (the Latin Library prints 'agnosco') — 'I recognise'; it governs the little Troy, the Pergama and the stream. 'Scaeaeque… portae' — the Scaean Gate of Troy, where Hector and Andromache parted in the Iliad (6.392–502); Aeneas embraces it as one embraces a relic.

sentences.t: Nec non et Teucri socia simul urbe fruuntur:
sentences.l: Nor not also the Teucrians the friendly city together enjoy:
sentences.i: My Trojans, too, were at the same time enjoying the friendly city:
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' — 'nor not also', a double negative that means 'and also' (litotes). 'Teucri' — the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer; the 'eu' is a single diphthong, so the word has two syllables, Teu-cri. 'socia… urbe' — 'fruor' takes an ablative, 'enjoy the friendly city'; 'socia' means 'allied, friendly'. 'simul' is an adverb, 'at the same time, together'. The present 'fruuntur' continues the narrative present. The colon introduces details of the welcome.

sentences.t: illos porticibus rex accipiebat in amplis;
sentences.l: them in porticoes the king was receiving, in spacious ones;
sentences.i: the king welcomed them in spacious colonnades;
sentences.n: 'illos… accipiebat' — 'accipio' is the word for receiving a guest; the imperfect 'accipiebat' sets the scene. 'rex' is Helenus. 'porticibus… in amplis' — a hyperbaton: the noun 'porticibus' and its adjective 'amplis' stand far apart, with 'rex accipiebat in' between them ('in porticoes… in spacious ones'). A portico is a covered colonnade.

sentences.t:
aulaï medio libabant pocula Bacchi,
impositis auro dapibus, paterasque tenebant.
sentences.l:
in the hall's midst they were pouring the cups of Bacchus,
the feasts set on gold, and they were holding the bowls.
sentences.i: In the middle of the hall they poured libations from cups of wine, with the dishes served on gold, and they held the sacrificial bowls in their hands.
sentences.n: 'aulaï' is an old genitive singular of 'aula' (in -ai), spelt with the diaeresis to show three syllables, au-la-i (as in 'Troïa'); it goes with 'medio', 'in the middle of the hall'. 'libabant pocula Bacchi' — 'libo' is 'to pour a libation, to sip as an offering', and 'pocula Bacchi' is 'cups of wine' (Bacchus is the wine-god, so metonymy). 'impositis auro dapibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the dishes having been set on gold'. 'paterasque tenebant' — 'paterae' were flat bowls for libations. The scene is a formal royal dinner in which the drinking is also an offering to the gods.

sentences.t:
Iamque dies alterque dies processit, et aurae
vela vocant tumidoque inflatur carbasus austro.
sentences.l:
And now a day and a second day advanced, and breezes
the sails call, and with swelling south wind is filled the canvas.
sentences.i: And now a day went by, and then another, and the breezes were calling the sails, and the canvas swelled with a billowing south wind.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iamque… processit' — 'processit' is a perfect, singular with two subjects ('dies alterque dies'), 'a day and another day went by'. 'aurae vela vocant' — the breezes call the sails, a personification. 'tumido… austro' — an ablative of means, 'with the swelling south wind' ('auster' is the south wind); 'inflatur carbasus' — 'the canvas is filled', the word for 'carbasus' being a Greek loan for fine cloth, here a sail. Two days pass in the feasting, and the wind now calls them on; this is the moment to consult the prophet.

sentences.t: His vatem adgredior dictis ac talia quaeso:
sentences.l: With these words I approach the seer and such things I ask:
sentences.i: With these words I go up to the seer and put this request to him:
sentences.n: 'His… dictis' — 'with these words', an ablative of means, with 'his' placed before 'vatem' for emphasis. 'vatem adgredior' — 'adgredior' is a deponent verb that takes an accusative, 'to approach, to address'; 'vatem' is 'the seer'. 'ac talia quaeso' — 'quaeso' here is 'I ask, I beg'. Helenus is a prophet of Apollo; in the Iliad he is the Trojan seer. A colon follows because the speech comes next.

sentences.t:
“Troiugena, interpres divom, qui numina Phoebi,
qui tripodas, Clarii laurus, qui sidera sentis,
et volucrum linguas et praepetis omina pennae,
sentences.l:
“Trojan-born, interpreter of the gods, you who the powers of Phoebus,
who the tripods, the laurels of the Clarian, who the stars perceive,
and the tongues of birds and the omens of the swift wing,
sentences.i: “Child of Troy, interpreter of the gods, who know the will of Phoebus, who know the tripods and the Clarian laurels, who read the stars, the speech of birds and the omens of a quick wing,
sentences.n: Aeneas's formal speech to Helenus. 'Troiugena' is a vocative, 'Troy-born' (a compound with the suffix -gena 'born'); 'interpres divom' — 'divom' is the old genitive plural of 'divus', 'of the gods' (-um or -om for -orum: you'll see this constantly), and 'interpres' (vocative) is 'interpreter, go-between'. 'qui… qui… qui… sentis' — a repeated relative clause (anaphora) with one verb at the end: 'you who know'; 'sentis' means 'perceive, understand'. 'numina Phoebi' — the divine will of Apollo; 'tripodas' (Greek accusative plural) are the tripods at the shrine at Delphi where the priestess sat; 'Clarii laurus' — 'Clarii' is the genitive singular of 'Clarius', 'the Clarian', a title of Apollo from his oracle at Claros; 'laurus' is an accusative plural (fourth declension); the laurel is Apollo's tree. 'sidera' = stars, 'volucrum linguas' = the language of birds (the augur's craft), 'praepetis… pennae' — 'praepetis' is the genitive singular of 'praepes', 'swift, flying straight', the word for an auspicious bird. In Greenough's line 360 there is no 'et' before the third 'qui'; the Latin Library prints one ('et qui sidera sentis'), but the sense is not changed.

sentences.t:
fare age—namque omnem cursum mihi prospera dixit
religio, et cuncti suaserunt numine divi
Italiam petere et terras temptare repostas:
sentences.l:
speak, come — for my whole course favourable things told
the sacred sign, and all the gods with divine will urged
to seek Italy and to try lands far-set:
sentences.i: speak, come now — for sacred omen has declared my whole voyage favourable, and every god by his divine will has urged me to make for Italy and to try remote lands:
sentences.n: 'fare age' — 'fare' is the imperative of the deponent 'for', 'speak', and 'age' is 'come on'. 'namque omnem cursum mihi prospera dixit religio' — 'religio' means the divine sign, the sacred omens (often in Virgil, the 'religious obligation'); 'dixit' with 'prospera' (neuter plural, 'favourable things') as a sort of cognate object: 'told favourable things (about) my whole voyage'. 'cuncti suaserunt numine divi' — 'numine' (ablative of means) 'by their divine will'; the nominative 'cuncti… divi' is 'all the gods'. 'Italiam petere et terras temptare repostas' — 'suaserunt' with two infinitives ('to seek… to try'); 'repostas' is 'repositas' by syncopation, 'remote, far-back'. The colon introduces the problem of the single unfavourable voice.

sentences.t:
sola novum dictuque nefas Harpyia Celaeno
prodigium canit, et tristis denuntiat iras,
obscenamque famem—quae prima pericula vito?
sentences.l:
alone a strange thing and, to say it, impious
portent Celaeno, the Harpy, sings, and grim wraths declares,
and foul hunger — which dangers first do I avoid?
sentences.i: only the Harpy Celaeno sings of a strange portent, wicked to utter, and proclaims grim wrath and loathsome hunger — which of the dangers must I avoid first?
sentences.n: The only voice against: 'sola… Harpyia Celaeno' is the subject, who 'sings' ('canit', here 'proclaims in prophecy') a portent ('prodigium'). 'novum dictuque nefas… prodigium' — the adjective 'novum' and the phrase 'dictu nefas' ('dictu' is a supine in -u, 'to say') frame the line; 'nefas' is 'wicked, forbidden'. Celaeno's prophecy was given in the last part (3.245–257). 'tristis… iras' — an accusative plural in -is; 'denuntiat' means 'announce, declare'. 'obscenamque famem' — 'obscenus' means 'ill-omened, foul'; the 'famem' is the hunger that will make them eat their tables. 'quae prima pericula vito?' — 'which dangers first do I avoid?'. A present indicative, but the question asks what he should do ('which must I avoid?').

sentences.t: Quidve sequens tantos possim superare labores?”
sentences.l: And by following what could I overcome such great labours?”
sentences.i: And by following what course could I get through such trials?”
sentences.n: 'Quidve' — 'quid' with '-ve', 'or what'. 'sequens' is a present participle, 'following'; the object of 'sequens' is 'quid', 'what (course)'. 'possim superare' — 'possim' is a present subjunctive in a question, 'could I', a deliberative or potential use. 'tantos… labores' — the labours are the whole voyage to Italy. The closing ” ends Aeneas's question to the seer.

sentences.t:
Hic Helenus, caesis primum de more iuvencis,
exorat pacem divom, vittasque resolvit
sacrati capitis, meque ad tua limina, Phoebe,
ipse manu multo suspensum numine ducit,
atque haec deinde canit divino ex ore sacerdos:
sentences.l:
Then Helenus, with steers first slain according to custom,
supplicates the peace of the gods, and the fillets looses
of his consecrated head, and me to your threshold, Phoebus,
himself by hand, in suspense with much divine power, leads,
and these things then sings from his divine mouth the priest:
sentences.i: Then Helenus, first slaying young bullocks as the rite requires, entreats the gods for peace, takes the fillets off his hallowed head, and with his own hand leads me, held in awe by the god's great presence, to your threshold, Phoebus; and from his inspired lips the priest speaks these words:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'caesis primum de more iuvencis' is an ablative absolute, 'the young bullocks (having been) slain first, as is the custom'. 'exorat pacem divom' — 'exoro' is to win by entreaty; 'pacem' is the peace (goodwill) of the gods, 'divom' the old genitive plural. 'vittasque resolvit sacrati capitis' — 'vittae' are the woollen fillets of a priest, 'resolvit' unbinds them, and 'sacrati' is a genitive from 'sacratus', 'consecrated'. 'meque ad tua limina, Phoebe' — Aeneas addresses the god directly in the middle of his narrative (apostrophe); he is speaking to Dido, but he turns aside to the god. 'multo suspensum numine' — 'suspensum' agrees with 'me' ('held in suspense, in awe'), and 'multo numine' means 'by the much divine presence'; Aeneas is awed to be at the god's shrine. 'divino ex ore' — 'ex' stands between the adjective and its noun; 'sacerdos' is the priest, Helenus. The colon opens the long prophecy that fills the rest of this part and the next.

sentences.t:
“Nate dea,—nam te maioribus ire per altum
auspiciis manifesta fides:
sentences.l:
“Son of a goddess — for that you go over the deep under greater
auspices, there is clear assurance:
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess — for it is clear beyond doubt that you sail the deep under higher auspices:
sentences.n: The prophecy begins with a long parenthesis. 'Nate dea' as at 310, 'son of a goddess' ('dea' is an ablative of origin). 'nam te maioribus ire per altum auspiciis manifesta fides' — 'manifesta fides' is the main clause with 'est' understood, 'clear is the assurance'; the 'te… ire' is an accusative and infinitive depending on 'fides' ('the assurance that you go…'); 'maioribus auspiciis' means 'under greater auspices', that is, under the omens of a higher power than ordinary mortals; 'altum' is 'the deep, the sea'. The opening mark “ opens Helenus's speech, which goes on into the next part.

sentences.t:
sic fata deum rex
sortitur, volvitque vices;
sentences.l:
thus the fates the king of the gods
allots, and rolls the changes;
sentences.i: that is how the king of the gods allots the fates and turns the changes of fortune;
sentences.n: 'sic' is the key: 'thus', as an explanation of the sentence just said. 'fata deum rex sortitur' — 'deum' is the old genitive plural (= 'deorum'), 'rex' is Jupiter; 'sortitur' ('allots, assigns by lot') is a deponent verb with 'fata' as its object; 'sors' is a lot. 'volvitque vices' — 'volvit' is 'rolls, unrolls', and 'vices' (plural) are 'turns, changes of fortune, succession'.

sentences.t: is vertitur ordo—
sentences.l: this order is turned —
sentences.i: such is the order of the turning —
sentences.n: 'is vertitur ordo' — 'is' (nominative, masculine) points back to what has been said, 'this order' ('ordo') 'is turned', that is, goes round. The dash closes the parenthesis that began at 'nam'. The main sentence, begun with 'Nate dea', is picked up in the next line with 'pauca tibi e multis… expediam'.

sentences.i: I shall set out for you in words a few things out of many, that you may cross the foreign seas more safely and be able to settle in an Italian harbour;
sentences.n: The main clause, held back by the parenthesis: 'pauca tibi e multis… expediam dictis' — 'pauca' ('a few things') is an object, 'e multis' ('out of many'), 'expediam' ('I shall unfold, set out'), 'dictis' ('in words', ablative of means). 'quo tutior… lustres… et… possis considere' — 'quo' with a comparative ('more safely') begins a purpose clause with the present subjunctives 'lustres' ('you may traverse') and 'possis' ('you may be able'); you'll see this constantly. 'hospita aequora' — 'hospita' means 'foreign, strange, unfamiliar' here (not 'hospitable'); 'Ausonio… portu' — Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy, and 'portu' is an ablative of place. 'considere' is 'to settle, sit down, come to rest'.

sentences.t:
prohibent nam cetera Parcae
scire Helenum farique vetat Saturnia Iuno.
sentences.l:
for the rest the Fates forbid
Helenus to know and Saturnian Juno forbids him to say.
sentences.i: for the Fates forbid Helenus to know the rest, and Saturnian Juno forbids him to say it.
sentences.n: 'prohibent nam cetera Parcae scire Helenum' — 'nam' is postponed to the second place, 'for'; 'cetera' ('the rest') is the object of 'scire'; 'prohibent' with an accusative and infinitive ('they forbid Helenus to know'). 'farique vetat Saturnia Iuno' — a second verb, 'vetat' ('forbids'), with an infinitive 'fari' (the deponent 'for', again), and the object 'Helenum' is understood from the first. 'Saturnia Iuno' — Juno is daughter of Saturn. Two limits are set on the prophecy: the Fates keep the rest from Helenus' knowledge, and Juno forbids him to speak.

sentences.t:
Principio Italiam, quam tu iam rere propinquam
vicinosque, ignare, paras invadere portus,
longa procul longis via dividit invia terris.
sentences.l:
First, Italy, which you now think near
and neighbouring harbours, unknowing, are preparing to enter,
a long way, far off, pathless, with long lands divides.
sentences.i: First: Italy, which you suppose already near, whose neighbouring harbours you, in your ignorance, are getting ready to enter: a long pathless road, far away, divides it from you with long stretches of land.
sentences.n: 'Principio' (ablative) is 'at the start, first of all'. 'Italiam, quam tu iam rere propinquam' — 'rere' is 'reris', the second person singular present of the deponent 'reor', 'think'; 'propinquam' agrees with 'Italiam'. 'vicinosque, ignare, paras invadere portus' — 'ignare' is a vocative ('you who do not know'); 'paras' ('you prepare') takes an infinitive 'invadere' ('to enter, to go into'). 'longa procul longis via dividit invia terris' — 'Italiam' is the object of 'dividit' ('divides it from you'): a pathless ('invia') long road ('via') divides it, far off ('procul'), with long lands ('longis terris', ablative of means); the repetition 'longa… longis' reproduces the length it describes. Aeneas thinks Italy is close; Helenus tells him it is not.

sentences.t:
Ante et Trinacria lentandus remus in unda,
et salis Ausonii lustrandum navibus aequor,
infernique lacus, Aeaeaeque insula Circae,
quam tuta possis urbem componere terra:
sentences.l:
First both in Trinacrian wave must the oar be bent,
and the Ausonian salt's expanse must be traversed by ships,
and the infernal lakes, and the isle of Aeaean Circe,
before you can found a city on safe land:
sentences.i: First you must bend your oar in Sicilian water, and cross by ship the salt expanse of the Italian sea, and pass the lakes of the underworld and the island of Circe of Aeaea, before you can found a city on safe ground:
sentences.n: 'Ante… quam' is split in two (tmesis), 'ante' at the start of 384 and 'quam' in 387: 'before… you can found'. 'lentandus remus' — 'lentandus' is a gerundive, 'to be bent, strained' (the oar flexes in the water), and with 'est' understood it expresses obligation. 'Trinacria… unda' — Trinacria is Sicily, 'the three-cornered island'. 'salis Ausonii lustrandum navibus aequor' — also a gerundive, 'must be traversed'; 'salis… aequor' is 'the level of the salt', that is, the sea. 'infernique lacus' — the lakes of the underworld, i.e. Avernus: the journey will take Aeneas to the underworld in Book VI. 'Aeaeaeque insula Circae' — 'Aeaeae' is the genitive singular feminine of the adjective 'Aeaeus', agreeing with 'Circae' (Greenough prints 'Aeaeaeque'); Circe's island Aeaea is the place in the Odyssey. 'tuta… terra' — an ablative of place, 'on safe ground'. Aeneas reaches Sicily in Book V and the underworld in Book VI, and passes Circe's island at the opening of Book VII.

sentences.t: signa tibi dicam, tu condita mente teneto:
sentences.l: signs to you I shall tell, you stored in the mind hold:
sentences.i: I shall give you signs; keep them stored in your mind:
sentences.n: 'dicam' is the future, 'I shall tell'. 'condita' is a perfect passive participle, neuter plural agreeing with 'signa', 'stored away'. 'teneto' is a future imperative (the ending -to), the solemn form for commands in laws and oracles: 'you shall hold'. 'tu' is the emphatic subject. Helenus stresses that this part of the prophecy must be remembered.

sentences.t:
cum tibi sollicito secreti ad fluminis undam
litoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus sus
triginta capitum fetus enixa iacebit.
alba, solo recubans, albi circum ubera nati,
is locus urbis erit, requies ea certa laborum.
sentences.l:
when to you, anxious, by a secluded river's wave
under shore-side holm-oaks a huge sow, found,
of thirty heads a litter having borne, will lie,
white, on the ground reclining, white around her teats the young,
that will be the place of the city, that the sure rest from your labours.
sentences.i: When, in your anxiety, by the water of a secluded river, you find a huge sow lying beneath the holm-oaks of the bank, white, stretched on the ground, her litter of thirty young beside her, white about her teats, that place will be the site of your city, that your sure rest from your labours.
sentences.n: The print has a full stop after 'iacebit' (line 391), a misprint for a comma, corrected here: 'alba' (392) is lower-case and in apposition to 'sus', and the sentence runs on to 'is locus urbis erit'. The Latin is left as printed, the unit runs on across the stop, and the translation reads the comma. 'cum tibi sollicito' — 'cum' with the future 'iacebit', 'when… will lie'; 'tibi sollicito' is a dative of the person concerned ('you, anxious'). 'secreti' is 'set apart, secluded'. 'litoreis… ilicibus' — 'ilex' is the holm-oak. 'ingens inventa… sus' — 'inventa' is a perfect passive participle, 'found' (by you). 'triginta capitum fetus enixa' — 'capitum' is a genitive of description, 'of thirty heads', 'enixa' (from 'enitor') is a perfect participle meaning 'having given birth to', and 'fetus' is the litter. 'alba… albi… nati' — the white sow and her white young; Alba Longa, the city founded by Ascanius, is named for this white (8.43–48 repeats the prodigy), and the thirty piglets are the thirty years until the founding. 'is locus urbis erit' — 'is' is 'that', and 'urbis' is a genitive of possession used predicatively, 'will be the city's'; 'ea' agrees with 'requies', 'that (will be) the sure rest'.

sentences.t: Nec tu mensarum morsus horresce futuros:
sentences.l: And you the tables' bites do not dread, future ones:
sentences.i: And do not shrink from the gnawing of the tables that is to come:
sentences.n: 'Nec… horresce' — a poetic negative command with 'nec' and the imperative (the usual prose form is 'noli horrescere'); 'horresco' takes an accusative, 'to shudder at'. 'mensarum morsus' — the 'bites of the tables', the prophecy of Celaeno (3.255–257) that hunger would force them to eat their tables. In Book VII the Trojans eat their bread-plates (the tables), Ascanius notices it in jest, and Aeneas sees the promise fulfilled. 'futuros' is a future participle, 'about to be', agreeing with 'morsus'. Helenus is reassuring the man who has asked, in line 367, about 'obscenam famem'.

sentences.t: fata viam invenient, aderitque vocatus Apollo.
sentences.l: the fates will find a way, and Apollo will be present, called.
sentences.i: The fates will find a way, and Apollo, if called, will be at hand.
sentences.n: 'fata viam invenient' — 'invenient' is a future; the fates will find a way. 'aderitque vocatus Apollo' — 'adero' is 'to be present, to come to help'; 'vocatus' is a perfect passive participle with a condition in it ('if he is called'). Helenus speaks for Apollo, his own god.

sentences.i: But these lands, and this stretch of the Italian shore which lies nearest and is washed by the tide of our sea, you must flee;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Has autem terras' — 'autem' is postponed to the second place, 'but, moreover'. 'Italique hanc litoris oram' — 'Italique' (genitive, going with 'litoris') is separated from its noun by 'hanc', which goes with 'oram': 'this edge of the Italian shore'. 'proxuma' (Greenough's spelling of 'proxima') is 'nearest'. 'perfunditur' — a present passive, 'is washed over', with 'aestu' ('by the tide', ablative of means). 'nostri aequoris' — 'our sea' is the Ionian, which runs between Greece and the Italian heel. The word that has all the meaning is 'effuge', the imperative, held until the end of the clause; the coast opposite Epirus, the part of Italy Aeneas would reach first, is the one he must avoid.

sentences.t: cuncta malis habitantur moenia Grais.
sentences.l: all the cities are inhabited by wicked Greeks.
sentences.i: every city there is inhabited by wicked Greeks.
sentences.n: 'cuncta… moenia' — 'moenia', 'walls', stands for cities. 'habitantur' — passive, 'are inhabited'; 'malis… Grais' is an ablative of agent without a preposition (a poetic extension; prose has 'a'), 'by wicked Greeks'. 'Graius' is the poetic word for 'Greek'. 'malis' means 'wicked, hostile', that is, the Greeks who destroyed Troy. The next lines name the settlements.

sentences.i: Here the Locrians from Naryx have set up their walls, and Idomeneus of Lyctus has occupied the Sallentine plains with his troops;
sentences.n: 'Narycii Locri' — the Locrians of Naryx, in Greece, led by the lesser Ajax, who settled in southern Italy (Locri Epizephyrii). 'posuerunt moenia' — 'they placed walls', that is, 'founded cities'. 'Sallentinos… campos' — the territory of the Sallentini, in Calabria (the heel of Italy). 'obsedit milite' — 'obsedit' means 'beset, occupied' and 'milite' is the collective singular 'soldiery', ablative of means. 'Lyctius Idomeneus' — Idomeneus, the king of Crete (Lyctus is a Cretan city), who, according to the tradition, was driven out of Crete and settled in Italy.

sentences.t:
hic illa ducis Meliboei
parva Philoctetae subnixa Petelia muro.
sentences.l:
here that little Petelia of the Meliboean leader
Philoctetes, propped on a wall.
sentences.i: Here, too, is the little town of Petelia, held up by its wall, of Philoctetes the Meliboean leader.
sentences.n: 'hic illa… parva… Petelia' — 'illa' means 'that famous', and the verb ('est', 'stands') is left out. 'ducis Meliboei Philoctetae' — 'Meliboei' is the genitive singular of the adjective 'Meliboeus', 'of Meliboea' (a town in Thessaly), and 'Philoctetae' is a Greek genitive in apposition to 'ducis', hyperbaton because the two stand in different lines: 'of the leader Philoctetes of Meliboea'. He was the owner of Hercules's bow, left on Lemnos, and in the tradition founded Petelia in Bruttium. 'subnixa… muro' — 'subnixa' is a perfect participle, 'supported, propped', with 'muro' (ablative), 'on a wall'; a little town that depends on its wall alone.

sentences.t:
Quin, ubi transmissae steterint trans aequora classes,
et positis aris iam vota in litore solves,
purpureo velare comas adopertus amictu,
ne qua inter sanctos ignis in honore deorum
hostilis facies occurrat et omina turbet.
sentences.l:
Moreover, when your fleets, having crossed, shall have stood across the seas,
and altars set up now your vows on the shore you pay,
veil your hair, covered with a purple mantle,
lest any hostile face among the holy fires
in the honour of the gods occur and disturb the omens.
sentences.i: And besides: when your fleets have crossed and lie at anchor, and you have set up altars and are paying your vows on the shore, veil your hair, wrapped in a purple mantle, so that no hostile face may meet you among the holy fires, in the honour paid to the gods, and spoil the omens.
sentences.n: 'Quin' introduces a further command, 'moreover, what is more'. 'ubi… steterint… solves' — 'ubi' ('when') begins the clause: 'steterint' is a future perfect, 'shall have stood', and 'solves' a future, 'you will pay'. 'transmissae… classes' — 'transmissae' is a perfect passive participle, 'having crossed over'. 'positis aris' is an ablative absolute. 'solves vota' — 'to pay a vow' is the usual phrase. 'purpureo velare comas adopertus amictu' — 'velare' is best taken as a passive (middle) imperative, 'cover yourself', with 'comas' an accusative of respect ('as to your hair', a Greek construction); 'adopertus' ('covered over') then repeats the idea, with 'amictu' ('with a mantle', ablative of means). Some read 'velare' as an infinitive used for a command; the sense is the same. Covering the head at sacrifice was the Roman custom, as against the Greek practice of sacrificing bareheaded, so Virgil gives the practice of his own day a Trojan origin. 'ne qua… facies occurrat et omina turbet' — a negative purpose clause ('ne qua' means 'lest any'), the subjunctives 'occurrat' ('may meet') and 'turbet' ('may disturb'); 'inter sanctos ignis' — 'ignis' is an accusative plural in -is, 'among the holy fires'. The 'hostilis facies' is an unfriendly face, one that would be an evil omen and spoil the rite.

sentences.t: Hunc socii morem sacrorum, hunc ipse teneto:
sentences.l: This custom of rites your comrades, this yourself, hold:
sentences.i: Let your companions keep this custom of the rites, and keep it yourself:
sentences.n: 'Hunc… hunc' — anaphora, 'this (custom)… this (custom)'. 'morem sacrorum' — 'the usage of the rites'. 'socii' (nominative) has to borrow its verb from 'teneto', a future imperative addressed to Aeneas himself ('ipse'): 'let your companions hold (it), hold it yourself'. The colon prepares the last command.

sentences.t: hac casti maneant in religione nepotes.
sentences.l: in this observance chaste may remain the descendants.
sentences.i: In this observance may your descendants remain pure.
sentences.n: 'maneant' is a present subjunctive of wish, 'may they remain'. 'hac… in religione' — 'in this observance, this religious practice' (the preposition stands between the demonstrative and its noun). 'casti' means 'pure, ritually clean'. 'nepotes' are 'descendants' (the sense is wider than 'grandsons'), that is, the Romans; the veiled head is the ritus Romanus. Helenus's speech goes on in the next part, so there is no closing mark here.
